UNITED STATES OF AMERICA  
BEFORE THE  
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION  
 
 
PJM Interconnection, LLC  
)

Docket No. ER 26-3380
 
 
 
LIMITED PROTEST OF PUBLIC INTEREST ORGANIZATIONS 
 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”),1 Sierra Club and Natural Resources 
Defense Council (“NRDC”) (collectively, “Public Interest Organizations” or “PIOs”) submit this 
limited protest of one aspect of PJM Interconnection, LLC’s (“PJM”) proposed Reliability 
Backstop Procurement (“RBP”).2 For the reasons described below, PIOs urge the Commission to 
approve PJM’s RBP Filing with a modification to either require RBP supply to be located near to 
large loads, or to require RBP supply to be fully responsible for funding necessary network 
upgrades, which will enable the RBP to better achieve its intended objectives.  
Introduction 
 
The unprecedented number of new large load additions, mostly data centers, in the PJM 
footprint has outstripped new supply, and PJM’s capacity auctions have cleared short of the 
region’s reliability requirement for consecutive auctions despite hitting auction price caps in both 
auctions.3 These shortfalls increase the risk of loss-of-load events and sustained high-capacity

prices for existing ratepayers who are not responsible for these new shortfalls. The RBP is an 
attempt by PJM to remedy these shortfalls without shifting costs to residential and other existing 
ratepayers. PJM proposes a one-time procurement of new capacity sized to the 2028/2029 
shortfall, with costs that will be allocated to the zones and load-serving entities (“LSEs”) serving 
the new large loads that are driving the unprecedented new demand.4 PIOs generally support 
PJM’s proposal to procure new capacity and allocate costs to the large loads that require it. 
 
PIOs support many aspects of the RBP Filing. For example, PJM is admirably candid 
about the fact that the capacity shortfalls are “primarily driven by the unprecedented addition of 
large loads, most notably data centers.”5 PJM also takes seriously and attempts to realize the 
Ratepayer Protection Pledge, in which the nation’s largest data center developers and utilities 
committed to “build, bring, or buy” the new generation their new demand requires and to pay 
“the full cost of those resources.”6 In an effort to ensure that costs of the RBP are borne by the 
large loads, PJM structured the RBP charges, which are reduced by Qualifying RBP Offsets 
where load has already procured its own new capacity,7 to flow to the zones where the new large 
loads are being built under a load-adjustment methodology that the Commission has already 
approved.8 PJM’s proposal achieves this cost allocation while respecting state jurisdiction by

and retail regulatory authorities are able to assign costs appropriately.9  
 
PJM’s consent to modification is a further signal that it is committed to the most effective 
RBP possible. Rather than a present a take-it-or-leave-it package, PJM “consents to the 
Commission’s exercise of authority to modify and/or sever any element of the proposed Tariff 
and RAA language,” so long as any modification “is consistent with PJM’s overarching 
objectives in this filing.”10 PJM invites stakeholders to “comment as they feel necessary and 
appropriate.”11 PIOs accept this invitation by proposing a narrow but important modification that 
the Commission can prescribe in an order approving the RBP. 
 
PJM’s consent is bounded by its “overarching objectives in this filing,” yet the RBP 
Filing never defines these objectives explicitly.12 Fairly read, however, the RBP pursues four 
objectives: 
1. Identify and procure the correct amount of capacity; 
2. Procure new capacity that is additive to the PJM system, not a mere reshuffling of 
existing resources; 
3. Procure new capacity on time; and  
4. Ensure that the large loads that require new capacity bear their full costs without shifting 
costs to other ratepayers and while preserving state authority over retail cost allocation. 
 
This limited protest identifies a narrow but important modification that will help the RBP 
advance these objectives. PJM’s proposal currently lacks any requirement regarding the location

of RBP supply. Instead, PJM argues that RBP resources may be located anywhere in the region 
because the interconnection process will ensure that supply is initially deliverable to load, and 
the regional transmission planning process will ensure that supply remains deliverable over the 
long term. However, as discussed below, PJM’s proposal to allow RBP supply to be located 
anywhere in the footprint will make the RBP’s success reliant on large-scale network upgrades 
that will likely cause significant delays and incur significant costs. Further, the interconnection 
process and regional transmission process risk inappropriately spreading the costs of network 
upgrades to other interconnection customers and ratepayers, rather than achieving the goal of the 
RBP—and the goals of federal and state policies—to require large loads to bear their own costs. 
To remedy this defect, this protest respectfully recommends that the Commission modify the 
RBP filing by either requiring RBP supply to be located near to demand, or by requiring RBP 
supply resources to be fully responsible for the cost of network upgrades. Such a modification 
will reduce reliance on large, slow, costly network upgrades and better achieve the RBP’s 
objectives of bringing new supply online quickly and facilitating appropriate allocation of costs 
to LSEs serving new large loads.  
 
Importantly, this modification will disturb neither the RBP’s architecture nor its schedule, 
and falls squarely within PJM’s consent. This modification will help the RBP procure the new 
capacity the region needs, where it needs it, with costs borne by the large loads that require it.  
Background 
I. 
PJM’s capacity market is facing reliability and affordability concerns as PJM 
struggles to meet data center load growth.   
 
 
PJM’s capacity market, the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”), worked relatively well 
for the two decades since it was first established in 2006. Its market was built for predictable, 
gradual load growth where new generation resources could be built within the market’s three-

5 
 
year forward timeline.13 However, as load growth, generation retirement, and supply chain 
development time have all increased in the past few years, PJM has recognized that the current 
state of its market is untenable.14 PJM’s markets are facing two major pain points: (1) data center 
load is growing too fast for PJM’s supply, leading to reliability concerns; and (2) PJM’s supply 
and demand imbalance is causing high capacity prices, leading to higher bills for all ratepayers.  
A. 
PJM’s capacity market faces increased reliability risks as data center load 
grows too quickly for PJM’s supply.  
 
  
First, PJM’s market is facing unprecedented load growth from rising data center demand, 
causing major supply and demand imbalances and increased reliability risks. Markets across the 
U.S. have not experienced this level of demand growth in decades. Electricity demand in the 
U.S. was relatively flat from the early 2000s until the early 2020s.15 That trend has quickly 
changed. Over the next five years, the U.S. is expecting electricity usage to grow 5.7% per 
year.16 Data centers are expected to make up 25% to 55% of the total demand growth in the U.S.

Most data center load growth through 2030 will be concentrated in the Electric

MW for its winter peak.22

As a result of its supply and demand imbalance, PJM has fallen short of its reliability

B. 
PJM’s capacity market faces high capacity prices, causing increases in 
ratepayers’ bills.  
 
 
Second, in addition to facing increased reliability risks, PJM’s market is also facing 
unsustainably high prices. The past three BRAs cleared at the price cap, clearing at $325/MW-
day in the 2028/2029 BRA, $333.44/MW-day in the 2027/2028 BRA, and $329.17/MW-day in 
the 2026/2027 BRA. For reference, PJM’s 2024/2025 BRA cleared at $28.92/MW-day and at 
$269.92/MW-day in the 2025/2026 BRA.30 PJM’s independent market monitor (IMM) estimated 
that data centers caused 63% of the increase in prices in the 2025/2026 BRA, resulting in an 
increase of $9.3 billion in higher costs for PJM customers.31 As of January 2026, the IMM 
estimated that the costs to other customers increased by $23 billion as a result of data center 
demand in the 2025/2026, 2026/2027, and 2027/2028 BRAs.32  
 
PJM’s increased capacity costs are raising ratepayers’ bills. In June 2025, Pepco 
customers in Washington, D.C. saw their bills increase by $21 per month, and D.C.’s Office of 
Consumers’ Counsel attributed about half of that increase to the spike in capacity market 
prices.33 Similar trends are expected across PJM. In June 2026, PJM customers collectively 
began paying an additional $1.4 billion in capacity market costs driven by data center demand.34

The increase in PJM’s capacity market prices has sparked concern from the White House, 
the 13 PJM states, the PJM board, and from data center companies themselves. On January 15, 
2026, the White House’s National Energy Dominance Council and the governors of the PJM 
states signed a joint Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, urging PJM to hold a Reliability 
Backstop Auction to procure new capacity resources for data centers and allocate the costs of 
that new capacity to Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”) with new data centers that have not 
procured their own capacity.35 Similarly, on January 16, the PJM board released a board 
decisional letter that directed PJM staff to develop several proposals to address reliability and 
affordability challenges caused by large load additions in PJM.36 Like the White House and PJM 
Governors’ Statement of Principles, PJM’s board urged PJM staff to initiate a Reliability 
Backstop Procurement and address cost allocation for LSEs that are short as a result of load 
growth in their service areas.37 
 
Lastly, the largest AI data center companies and developers in the country signed the 
White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge—introduced on March 4, 2026, and expanded in 
July—a voluntary commitment from data center owners to build, bring, or buy the new 
generation resources needed to satisfy their new energy demands and pay the full cost of those 
resources.38

II. 
PJM’s Reliability Backstop Proposal should be accepted with modifications to better 
achieve the RBP’s objectives. 
 
PIOs generally support PJM’s Reliability Backstop Procurement proposal but urge the 
Commission to exercise its authority to modify the proposal to better accomplish PJM’s 
objectives to: (1) procure the correct amount of capacity to meet the RBP target; (2) procure new 
capacity; (3) procure that new capacity on time; and (4) ensure that large loads that require new 
capacity bear the costs of building and connecting that capacity. Specifically, the Commission 
should accept PJM’s proposal, but only on the conditions that PJM either require RBP supply to 
be located near to large loads, which will help ensure that new supply can come online timely, 
and that reliability risks or costs associated with delivering new RBP capacity to large loads are 
not shifted to other ratepayers, or require RBP resources to cover 100% of network upgrades. 
Additionally, the Commission should encourage states to mandate take-or-pay agreements 
between LSEs and large loads to mitigate the risks of cost-shifting if a data center fails to 
materialize as expected.  
Discussion 
 
I. 
The Commission Should Only Modify PJM’s RBP Filing to Better Accomplish 
PJM’s Objectives. 
 
PJM has consented to Commission modification of “any element” of its proposal, so long 
as the modification is “consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives in this filing.”39 That 
consent is bounded by the decision in NRG Power Marketing v. FERC to not permit 
modifications that would produce “an entirely different rate design.”40 PJM’s objectives set the 
limits of what modifications the Commission can require. However, the RBP Filing does not 
 
39 RBP Filing, supra note 2, at 130–31. 
40 NRG Power Mktg. LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 115–16 (D.C. Cir. 2017).

include any explicit statement of PJM’s objectives. To assist the Commission’s consideration of 
modifications to PJM’s filing, PIO’s explain that the text and context of PJM’s filing reveal the 
following four objectives. 
First, procure the correct amount of capacity. PJM explains that “the primary purpose of 
the RBP Target is to determine how much UCAP MW is needed to meet the reliability 
requirement shortfall without over-procuring,”41 and the PJM Board directed the target equal the 
2028/2029 shortfall, reduced for documented bilateral contracts and self-supply arrangements for 
new capacity serving new load.42  
Second, procure new capacity. The RBP “is designed to attract new supplies of capacity 
(i.e., new ICAP), not merely incremental resource efficiencies.”43  
Third, procure new capacity on time. While the contracts are for 15 years to incentivize 
new generation,44 the need for new capacity is urgent, and therefore, the timely procurement of 
capacity is an objective of PJM’s filing.45 PJM’s ranking of offers “from earliest to latest offered 
Delivery Year” even before considering cost shows PJM’s commitment to solving the immediate 
capacity need.46  
Fourth, ensure that the large loads that require the new capacity bear its costs. The RBP 
Filing invokes the Ratepayer Protection Pledge’s commitment that large loads will pay the “full

PIOs respectfully recommend that the Commission adopt this articulation of the RBP’s 
objectives and use those objectives when requiring modifications to the RBP. 
A. 
Objective One: Procure the Correct Amount of Capacity 
 
The RBP’s quantity of procured megawatts is set by administrative decision, not by 
market clearing. In the RPM auctions, the amount of capacity procured emerges from an 
administratively established demand curve interacting with competitive offers. Because the RPM 
is annual, the amount of capacity procured is revised annually and therefore responds to changes 
in the market. The RBP has no comparable self-correction. PJM sets the target, reduces it for 
verified Qualifying RBP Offsets and opt-outs, and procures the final number under fifteen-year 
commitments.48 Any over- or under-procurement is therefore locked in for fifteen years. Under-
procurement of new capacity leaves a reliability gap the RBP is designed to fix, which leaves 
customers exposed to increase loss-of-load risk. Over-procurement would mean that the 
participating zones and LSEs are stuck with fifteen years of charges for capacity they don’t need. 
PJM describes “the primary purpose of the RBP Target” as determining “how much UCAP MW 
is needed to meet the reliability requirement shortfall without over-procuring,” and it built the 
matching rules to “avoid[] over-procurement, under-procurement, and double-counting.”49 
In evaluating the RBP and any modifications proposed in this protest and by other parties, the 
Commission should ensure that the RBP procure the right amount of needed capacity. A

modification that improves the correspondence between the quantity procured and the shortfall 
that actually exists advances this objective and falls squarely within PJM’s consent. 
B. 
Objective Two: Procure New Capacity 
 
The second objective recognizes that the shortfall was due to a lack of steel in the ground 
supply rather than a mispricing of existing megawatts of supply. The need for genuinely new 
supply is recognized by the PJM Board, the Governors’ Principles, and the Ratepayer Protection 
Pledge. The RBP, therefore, “is designed to attract new supplies of capacity (i.e., new ICAP), not 
merely incremental resource efficiencies, to address the current capacity shortfall and a provide 
stable, long-term source of capacity.”50 If, for example, the RBP merely allowed existing 
resources to move from the RPM to the RBP, the entire process would be an exercise in wealth 
transfers with no reliability benefits. Genuinely additive procurement, by contrast, protects 
existing customers from paying for reliability problems they did not cause while also providing 
new load with long-term sources of generation. 
The Commission should therefore make additionality a core touchstone as it evaluates the 
RBP Proposal and any proposed modification. The Commission should ask: does the resource 
add installed capacity that the system did not have before? A modification that admits 
demonstrably additive resources enlarges the pool of new supply and advances the objective 
while increasing competition, improving speed to power, and lowering costs. A modification that 
would relax the screen against reshuffled or paper capacity is contrary to the objective and 
therefore should be dismissed by the Commission.

C. 
Objective Three: Procure New Capacity on Time 
 
The third objective recognizes that the need for new capacity is based on an existing 
shortfall, not a mere trend or forecast. The 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 auctions have already 
cleared short, and capacity is valuable for reliability only when it is installed. Supply arriving in 
2035 does nothing for loss-of-load risk in 2029. The RBP Proposal recognizes this urgency in its 
selection criteria. The RBP only allows projects that can demonstrate a feasible commercial 
operation date of June 1, 2032, or earlier.51 Once it collects all eligible projects, PJM then selects 
offers “in rank order from earliest to latest offered Delivery Year,” and only then by levelized 
cost. This means that PJM is willing to pay a higher price for capacity that arrives sooner.52 
Timeliness of projects is also important because PJM proposes to reset the trigger for the 
Tariff’s pre-existing Reliability Backstop Auction so that no such auction can occur unless BRAs 
clear short for three consecutive Delivery Years beginning with 2032/2033. PJM justifies this by 
assuming that “all RBP Resources should have reached their respective commercial operational 
dates” by that delivery year.53 The Commission should, therefore, recognize that significant 
reliability risks hang on the ability of the RBP to actually procure new supply in the next few 
years. 
The Commission should therefore treat speed to power as a key objective when 
evaluating the RBP Proposal and any proposed modifications. Where the Commission finds that 
the RBP will not actually bring new supply online quickly, it should require changes. Where a 
modification would improve speed to power, the Commission should consider adopting such

resources that can be rapidly deployed or that tolerate slippages in commercial operation date.  
D. 
Objective Four: Ensure That the Large Loads That Require New Capacity 
Bear Its Costs. 
 
PJM and its stakeholders recognize that new large loads, especially data centers, are 
uniquely responsible for the failure of recent auctions to clear at desired reserve margins. This 
failure to meet reliability standards puts everyone in the PJM footprint in danger of increased 
loss-of-load events. The RBP is designed to shore up that shortfall through new supply. Because 
these new costs are so clearly and uniquely caused by the massive expansion of data centers and 
similar new large loads, cost causation principles require that the RBP allocate costs to those new 
large loads. This is not a controversial position. The nation’s largest data center developers 
pledged to pay the “full cost” of the new resources their demand requires.54 The thirteen PJM 
governors pledged to direct these costs to “new data center loads that have not otherwise 
procured capacity or agreed to be curtailable.”55 PJM promises that RBP costs “will not become 
stranded costs, which would ultimately be socialized.”56 It is therefore crucial that the RBP fulfill 
its objective of ensuring that new large loads actually pay for the new supply they need. 
The Commission should apply this objective when evaluating the RBP and any proposed 
modifications. Commission and PJM jurisdiction over ratemaking, however, extends only so far. 
States set retail rates, which are actually charged to individual ratepayers—be they residential 
customers or data centers—for capacity charges assigned to LSEs by PJM. It is therefore

loads that are responsible for the need for this new supply procured through the RBP. The 
Commission should reject any component of the RBP that fails to sufficiently meet this cost

Taken together, the four objectives listed above state what PJM designed the RBP to do: 
procure the correct amount of new capacity, on time, at the cost of the large loads that require it. 
The Commission should evaluate any proposed modifications to PJM’s RBP filing against these 
objectives and should adopt PIOs’ narrow modification described below, which will help ensure 
that the RBP meets PJM’s objectives. 
II. 
The Commission should modify the RBP by requiring RBP supply to be located new 
large loads in order to minimize delays and the risk of cost-shifting.  
 
To ensure that PJM accomplishes its objectives to procure the (1) correct amount of (2)

Cost-Shifts in the RBP violate the Commission’s June 18 Large 
Load Order.  
 
Second, the RBP is unjust and unreasonable because the proposal is inconsistent with the 
Commission’s Large Load Order. As described in the Commission’s June 18 Large Load Order, 
the Commission has a duty to address the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers that 
may result in unjust and unreasonable rates.99 PJM’s current RBP proposal will likely result in 
unjust and unreasonable rates by shifting RBP costs to other transmission customers through 
PJM’s interconnection process and through RTEP.  
The Commission’s June 18 Large Load Order preliminarily found PJM’s tariff to be 
unjust and unreasonable because it lacks adequate mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost 
shifting among transmission customers.100 The Commission is concerned that PJM’s tariff does 
not ensure that large load customers would be ultimately response for costs incurred to provide 
transmission service, including the cost of network upgrades.101 Additionally, the Commission is 
concerned about inefficient and unnecessary infrastructure development that leads to unjust and 
unreasonable rates through unnecessarily high network upgrade costs.102 
The RBP proposal confirms all the Order’s worries about PJM’s inadequate cost-shifting 
protections. To the Commission’s first concern, the RBP relies on the interconnection process 
and RTEP to ensure deliverability but includes no adequate mechanism to mitigate the cost-shifts 
associated with those processes. Stakeholders alerted PJM to these cost-shifting concerns in the 
proposal in stakeholder discussions, but PJM’s proposal does not address these issues. To the

100 Id. at P 66.

102 Id.

34 
 
second concern, the current RBP structure will not ensure that large load customers will be 
ultimately responsible for costs incurred to provide their transmission service. The RBP will 
likely spread higher costs to generators due to complex load deliverability studies and higher 
network upgrade costs for the cluster. Load will likely experience higher costs through RTEP as 
the RTEP will likely identify costly transmission upgrades to deliver capacity from RBP 
resources. In either case, end ratepayers are ultimately responsible for costs incurred to provide 
transmission service to data centers, not the data centers themselves. 
 Lastly, the lack of a locational requirement in the RBP will likely lead to inefficient and 
unnecessary infrastructure buildout. If the RBP procures RBP resources that are farther away 
from the LDA it will serve, PJM may need to build transmission infrastructure to get the capacity 
from the RBP resource to the LDA. This result is inefficient and unnecessary when there may be 
resources closer to the LDA that could serve the load. This procurement structure could lead to 
unnecessary build-out and unnecessary network upgrade costs, which as the Commission points 
out in its June 18 Order, would be unjust and unreasonable.  
III. 
The Commission should encourage PJM states to do their part in allocating costs to 
data centers.   
 
It is important to note, as PJM does in its filing, that states have a large part to play in 
ensuring that cost allocation at the retail level adequately allocates RBP costs to data centers 
receiving capacity from RBP resources. The Commission has acknowledged states’ role in cost 
allocation as well, stating in its June 18 Large Load Order that “states determine how 
Commission-approved rates are collected among the relevant retail consumers along with the 
rates for state-jurisdictional matters.”103 The PJM Governors affirmed this role in their Statement 
 
103 Id. at P 69.

35 
 
of Principles Regarding PJM, in which the 13 PJM governors agreed to use all available 
authorities to ensure that LSEs allocate the cost to procure new capacity through the RBP to new 
data center loads.104 States must take this responsibility seriously. If not, the states risk spreading 
RBP costs to all load. 
PJM’s filing states that the PJM states will have a central role in protecting their 
ratepayers from cost shifts from the RBP.105 The RBP relies on each of the states to refine cost 
allocation to determine which retail loads should be allocated the cost of the procurement.106 If 
states do not adopt adequate tariffs, costs from the RBP may be allocated to residential customers 
or small industrial or commercial customers.  
Under the current RBP proposal, LSEs that forecast data center load and procure capacity 
for that load in the RBP may be left with enormous costs if that forecasted load does not show 
up. Because PJM proposes that LSE defaults will result in the allocation of the defaulted costs to 
other LSEs hosting large loads, if one LSE cannot cover the stranded costs resulting from data 
centers failing to materialize, then the rest of the LSEs with RBP obligations may be left holding 
the bill. There is a real risk of this outcome occurring. The CEOs of Constellation Energy and 
Vistra Energy have both warned their investors about the risks of overbuilding.107 In a 2025 
earnings call, Vistra CEO James Burke stated that load “interconnect queues . . . may be 
overstated from three to five times what might actually materialize in regulated markets or

50% more demand than the tech industry is projecting.109 Similarly, in November 2025, experts 
estimated that utility forecasts were overstating data center load growth by almost 25 GW.110  
If LSEs submit inflated load forecasts for the RBP, there is a risk that PJM will over-
procure capacity for load that will never show up. Nevertheless, PJM will still allocate those 
MWs, and the cost responsibility, to those LSEs. For LSEs with data centers that fail to 
materialize, this cost responsibility could be burdensome. PJM is expected to pay up to $20 
billion for the RBP.111 LSEs can be expected to pay millions of dollars each year depending on 
their respective RBP allocations. If data centers fail to show up, LSEs will be left with 
millions—or even billions—of dollars in stranded costs. If an LSE has more data centers in its 
service area, it can allocate these costs among remaining data centers. However, if all the data 
center load in an LSE fails to materialize, ratepayers will foot the bill, or the LSE will have to 
default and spread their costs to other LSEs.  
The Maryland Office of People’s Counsel (“MD OPC”) has sounded the alarm on this 
issue, warning its state Public Service Commission (“PSC”) about the risks of failing to pass 
adequate cost allocation tariffs. In comments to the PSC on August 10, 2026, the MD OPC 
explains that customers in zones with RBP obligations will be responsible for RBP costs 
regardless of whether the large loads included in the utilities’ forecast materialize or are

To prevent this cost-shifting, the Commission should encourage states to require take-or-
pay agreements between LSEs and large load customers for any LSEs participating in the RBP 
and require PJM to provide states with enough information to properly allocate costs through 
those agreements. These recommendations are consistent with PJM’s objective to allocate RBP 
costs to data centers, the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and with the Commission’s June 18th

Some utilities have already begun to think about how these take-or-pay arrangements 
could be implemented. In comments to the MD PSC on August 10, 2026, the Joint Maryland 
Exelon Utilities115 urged the PSC to consider requiring an agreement to hold large loads 
accountable for capacity costs, similar to a Transmission Security Agreement (TSA), to protect

Commission should uplift these recommendations and encourage other states to develop similar

Security agreements like the ones mentioned by the Joint Maryland Exelon Utilities are 
consistent with PJM’s objective to allocate the costs of the capacity required to serve data centers 
to those data centers and the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. PJM acknowledges that the RBP is “a 
product of cooperative federalism” and that state participation will be needed to ensure the 
success of the RBP and to protect residential customers from cost-shifts.117 PJM emphasizes that 
the states have the jurisdiction to ensure that new large loads, and not residential or small 
industrial or commercial customers, are allocated the retail costs associated with the costs of 
RBP resources procured at the wholesale level. State-mandated take-or-pay contracts between 
LSEs and large load customers align exactly with this structure that PJM outlines in its filing. 
Take-or-pay contracts will ensure that costs at the wholesale level are sub-allocated directly to 
large-load customers, regardless of whether they materialize or not, thereby protecting residential 
and small industrial customers from cost-shifts.  
Additionally, take-or-pay agreements are in line with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge 
because data centers have pledged to pay the costs of their power, whether they use it or not. The 
companies that signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge have agreed to not only “procure the 
generation needed for their energy demand . . . and pay the full cost,” but to also “voluntarily 
negotiate new, separate rate structures with their utilities and state governments” and “pay those

rates for the power and infrastructure brought online for them—whether or not they actually use 
the electricity.”118 Take-or-pay agreements are consistent with this pledge because they will 
ensure that large loads will pay the cost of the capacity brought online for them whether or not 
the large load actually shows up. These agreements will ensure that data centers follow through 
on their pledge, instead of leaving residential ratepayers with the bill if data centers fail to 
materialize.  
Lastly, the take-or-pay agreements are consistent with the spirit of the Commission’s June 
18th Large Load Order, which addresses the risk of cost-shifting among transmission customers 
due to speculative requests.119 The Commission’s Order was concerned that speculative 
transmission service requests on behalf of large loads could result in cost-shifting among 
transmission customers.120 The Commission was concerned that other transmission customers 
may have to pay increased rates if an Eligible Customer takes less transmission service than 
anticipated because a large load is operating at a lower demand than anticipated or fails to 
materialize.121  
The Commission’s Order found that, to prevent these cost shifts, PJM’s tariff should 
require that PJM, the relevant transmission owner, and the Eligible Customer enter into a cost 
recovery agreement that requires the Eligible Customer to make a minimum contribution towards 
the transmission owner’s revenue requirement if the Eligible Customer takes less transmission 
service than anticipated because the large load did not materialize as planned.122 The

Commission preliminarily found that these cost-recovery agreements were necessary to ensure 
that Eligible Customers were responsible for paying the costs of large-load driven transmission, 
“rather than having those costs paid by other transmission customers that neither caused the need 
for nor benefit commensurately from” those transmission upgrades.123 
Take-or-pay contracts with respect to the RBP would work similarly to the cost-recovery 
agreements outlined in the Commission’s Order and would serve a similar purpose. Like 
speculative transmission service requests, speculative data center demand that fails to materialize 
could likely result in cost-shifts among PJM’s customers. If a data center fails to materialize as 
expected or fails to show up at all, other customers in that LSE, either other large load customers 
or non-large load ratepayers, will have to make up the costs, resulting in higher prices for those 
customers. An RBP cost-recovery agreement between LSEs and large loads would, like in the 
transmission context, protect residential customers from cost-shifts by mandating that large loads 
pay a minimum contribution towards an LSE’s RBP obligation if those large loads fail to 
materialize as expected. Like the cost-recovery agreements proposed in the Commission’s Order, 
take-or-pay agreements would ensure that the costs of capacity procured to service large loads 
would be paid by the large load that caused the need for the RBP, rather than the LSE’s other 
customers.  
To mandate these take-or-pay agreements, PJM states must have the information needed 
to allocate the RBP costs to the appropriate customers. In addition to preliminarily finding that 
PJM must develop cost-recovery agreements, the Commission’s Large Load Order also found 
that PJM must provide clear, timely, and detailed information on their website regarding 
Network Upgrades for Eligible Customers and information about the costs of those upgrades. 
 
123 Id.

41 
 
The Commission was concerned that PJM lacked adequate cost transparency measures to 
provide stakeholders with the information and visibility needed to allocate costs driven by large 
loads.124 The Commission found that the cost transparency measures it proposed in its Order will 
allow state public utility commissions and other state regulators to understand which costs are 
caused by which customers, so that they can allocate those costs to the appropriate retail 
customers.125 
 
Similarly detailed information will be necessary in the RBP context. States will need to 
have enough information about which large loads are associated with certain RBP costs to sub-
allocate those costs to large loads at the retail level. Like the Commission stated in its Large 
Load Order, PJM should be required to provide clear, timely, and detailed information about 
RBP costs to states to ensure that states have enough information to mandate take-or-pay 
agreements between LSEs and large loads that adequately ensure that large loads pay for the 
costs of RBP capacity procured on their behalf, whether or not they materialize as expected.  
Conclusion 
PJM’s RBP filing generally presents a just and reasonable mechanism to procure capacity 
for large loads that are currently causing a shortfall in PJM’s capacity market and to facilitate the 
allocation of costs to large loads while respecting state jurisdiction over retail rates. However, 
PJM’s failure to include any requirement as to the location of RBP supply resources will increase 
the RBP’s reliance on large, costly network upgrades that threaten to delay when supply can 
become deliverable to the large loads that need it. The modification described above to require 
RBP supply to either be located near to demand, or to be fully responsible for the cost of network

promptly and to allocate costs to large loads rather than shifting costs to others. Accordingly, 
PIOs respectfully request that the Commission approve the RBP filing with the modification 
described above.

Introduction
Background
I. PJM’s capacity market is facing reliability and affordability concerns as PJM struggles to meet data center load growth.
A. PJM’s capacity market faces increased reliability risks as data center load grows too quickly for PJM’s supply.
B. PJM’s capacity market faces high capacity prices, causing increases in ratepayers’ bills.
II. PJM’s Reliability Backstop Proposal should be accepted with modifications to better achieve the RBP’s objectives.
Discussion
I. The Commission Should Only Modify PJM’s RBP Filing to Better Accomplish PJM’s Objectives.
A. Objective One: Procure the Correct Amount of Capacity
B. Objective Two: Procure New Capacity
C. Objective Three: Procure New Capacity on Time
D. Objective Four: Ensure That the Large Loads That Require New Capacity Bear Its Costs.
II. The Commission should modify the RBP by requiring RBP supply to be located new large loads in order to minimize delays and the risk of cost-shifting.
A. PJM’s proposal to exclude a locational requirement for RBP generation bids could lead to reliability risks.
B. PJM’s proposal will unjustly and unreasonably shift costs to other interconnection customers or ratepayers.
1. The RBP will likely shift costs of network upgrades to other interconnection customers and to all PJM load.
2. The RBP will likely shift the costs to study RBP resources to other interconnection customers.
3. PJM’s proposal will unjustly and unreasonably shift costs to all PJM customers through RTEP.
4. The RBP risks cost shifts that are inconsistent with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the Commission’s Large Load Orders.
a. Cost-shifts in the RBP violate the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the Commission’s June 18th Large Load Orders.
b. Cost-Shifts in the RBP violate the Commission’s June 18 Large Load Order.
III. The Commission should encourage PJM states to do their part in allocating costs to data centers.
